title: Ontario Reformatory heritage district moves to planning phase
subtitle: Retirement community rezoning at Gordon and Arkell, trestle bridge talks with Infrastructure Ontario, and a sports council town hall.
overview: Council voted to move ahead with a Heritage Conservation District for the former Ontario Reformatory lands. Staff will now prepare a district plan under the Ontario Heritage Act {{vote:m2}}. The study's recommended boundary covers the entry landscape, main buildings, working farm areas, and quarry and rail corridor lands. The designation is meant to protect the site's heritage value while development planning continues for the area.

Council also directed staff to keep talking with Infrastructure Ontario about conserving the wooden trestle bridge on the property and to report back {{vote:m3}}. Delegates said the bridge is at risk of demolition and could serve as a trail link.

Separately, council approved a rezoning for a mixed-use retirement community at 1408 Gordon Street and 33-41 Arkell Road {{vote:m1}}. Councillors asked about pedestrian crossings and traffic signals on Gordon Street. Staff said construction on the Gordon Street improvements is expected to start in 2025.
A councillor also announced a March 23 town hall at City Hall about forming a Guelph Sports Council.

decisions.detail: Council approved the study's recommendations and directed staff to prepare a heritage conservation district plan for the Ontario Reformatory area.
Staff will continue discussions with Infrastructure Ontario on options for conserving the Trestle Bridge on the former reformatory property and report back to Council.

decisions.item: 1408 Gordon Street and 33-41 Arkell Road rezoning
decisions.detail: Council approved a zoning change to a specialized general apartment zone to allow a mixed-use retirement community, with no further public notice needed for minor modifications.

debate: Delegates supported the study and urged council to start the plan phase quickly. They cited the thoroughness of the consultant's work and concern about provincial policy changes affecting heritage protection.

A trail club delegate warned that the plan may not reach council until late 2024 or early 2025. That could leave the wooden trestle bridge at risk. The delegate argued a repair would be cheaper than a new crossing and would keep embodied carbon, and asked the city and the developer to tell Infrastructure Ontario that the bridge has value.
Councillors asked why the plan phase takes so long. The consultant said the time goes to consultation and to testing policies so they hold up on appeal, and that the timeline is normal.

On the Gordon Street rezoning, a councillor raised pedestrian safety for future retirement community residents who will rely on transit and walking. Staff said traffic signal warrants are not currently met at Gordon and Vaughan. They said a new complete streets guideline tool could weigh the crossing again during the Gordon Street improvements.
Staff said the earlier traffic study's assumption of signals at that intersection was hypothetical. They said not installing signals raises no significant concerns for queuing or collision risk.
